lead: Source coding assigns short binary words to likely symbols and longer words to rare symbols. A prefix code keeps every codeword from being the start of another, so the receiver decodes bit by bit with no separators. Shannon-Fano and Huffman both build such codes from a probability list; Huffman is the standard method. The average length L̄ in bits per symbol can approach the entropy H(X), never fall below it. File compression, image formats and voice codecs use these ideas daily.
prereq: You need Chapter 7.1 for entropy H(X) and information rate.

sections.h3: Prefix codes and the source coding theorem

blocks.text: A fixed-length code wastes bits when one symbol dominates. A source emits symbols with probabilities pᵢ. Give symbol i a binary codeword of length lᵢ bits. A prefix code has no codeword that is the start of another. The set {0, 10, 110, 111} is prefix-free. After reading 10, the receiver knows the symbol ended; it never needs to look ahead. Decoding is instant, one bit at a time.

The Kraft inequality says that for any binary prefix code, Σ 2<sup>−lᵢ</sup> ≤ 1, where lᵢ is the length in bits of the codeword for symbol i. It is necessary and sufficient for integer lengths. We state it without proof.

blocks.where: L̄ is the average codeword length in bits per symbol; pᵢ is the probability of symbol i; lᵢ is the length in bits of its codeword. H(X) is the entropy from Chapter 7.1, in bits per symbol.

H(X) is the source entropy in bits per symbol. H(X) ≤ L̄ for every prefix code. For one symbol at a time, some prefix code (Huffman is one) has L̄ < H(X) + 1. For a block of n symbols coded together, H(X) ≤ L̄ < H(X) + 1/n.

blocks.text: The source coding theorem says no prefix code can have L̄ below H(X). Some prefix code has L̄ less than H(X)+1 for one symbol at a time. Integer codeword lengths cause this gap; it vanishes only when all probabilities are powers of 1/2.

blocks.where: η is the coding efficiency, a pure ratio; H(X) and L̄ must use the same logarithm base, normally base 2. Redundancy is the fraction of average length not carrying entropy.

blocks.text: Shannon-Fano builds a code top-down by repeated splitting. The split rule uses total probability, not symbol count.

items: Sort the symbols in decreasing order of probability.
Split the sorted list into two groups so that the two group probabilities are as nearly equal as possible. Keep the original order inside each group.
Give every codeword in the top group a leading 0 and every codeword in the bottom group a leading 1, or the reverse. Fix the choice and keep it.
Repeat the split inside each group until a group has one symbol.
Read each codeword from the root to its leaf.

blocks.text: The split is a heuristic. A poor split gives a valid but longer code. Sorting matters; an unsorted list can lengthen many codewords. Ties can give different average lengths, so check the nearest splits.
Huffman builds a code bottom-up by merging the least likely symbols first. This keeps large probabilities near the root and gives them short words.

items: Make one leaf node for each symbol, labelled with its probability.
Take the two nodes with the smallest probabilities. Join them under a new parent whose probability is their sum.
Label one edge from the parent 0 and the other edge 1. The choice is arbitrary if kept consistent.
Put the new parent back into the list and remove the two children.
Repeat until one node remains. Its probability is 1.0.
Read each codeword from the root to its leaf.

blocks.text: The two least likely symbols become siblings at the greatest depth. A Huffman code is prefix-free by construction. Among binary prefix codes with integer lengths, it is optimal for the given probabilities. Ties can produce different codewords, but the average length remains optimal. A heap implementation runs in O(n log n) for n symbols.
Huffman coding is used in ZIP files, JPEG and MP3 bitstreams, and many network protocols. The receiver needs the symbol probabilities or a code table; practical formats send a compact table.

For the five-symbol source in the worked example, Huffman gives lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 and L̄ = 2.2 bits/symbol. A Shannon-Fano split of 0.4 against 0.6, then 0.2 against 0.4, then 0.2 against 0.2, then 0.1 against 0.1 gives the same lengths here. That match is not guaranteed for every source. When Shannon-Fano chooses a worse split, Huffman can be shorter.
Both methods approach the entropy bound from above. Neither can go below H(X). Arithmetic coding removes the integer-length gap and is used when the last few percent matter.

figure.caption: Huffman merges the two smallest probabilities first, then the next smallest, and reads each codeword from the root. The codeword lengths are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 4 bits, so L̄ = 2.2 bits/symbol for this source.

examples.question: A discrete memoryless source emits five symbols A, B, C, D and E with probabilities 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1 and 0.1. (a) Find the entropy H(X). (b) Build the Huffman code, merging the two smallest probabilities first, and break the 0.2 tie at the second step by merging C with DE. (c) Find the average codeword length L̄ and the coding efficiency η.
steps: Sort the probabilities: A = 0.4, B = 0.2, C = 0.2, D = 0.1, E = 0.1.
Entropy: H(X) = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ = 0.4 log₂(2.5) + 2(0.2 log₂ 5) + 2(0.1 log₂ 10).
Huffman step 1: merge D 0.1 and E 0.1 into DE with probability 0.2.
Huffman step 2: there is a tie at 0.2 among B, C and DE. Merge C with DE into CDE with probability 0.4.
Huffman step 3: merge B 0.2 and CDE 0.4 into BCDE with probability 0.6.
Huffman step 4: merge A 0.4 and BCDE 0.6 into the root 1.0.
Read codes: A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 1110, E = 1111. Lengths are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 4 bits.
examples.answer: H(X) = 2.12 bits/symbol, L̄ = 2.2 bits/symbol, and η = 96.5% for the Huffman code A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 1110, E = 1111.
examples.check:
import math
p = [0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1]
H = -sum(pi * math.log2(pi) for pi in p)
L = 0.4*1 + 0.2*2 + 0.2*3 + 0.1*4 + 0.1*4
eta = 100 * H / L
print(round(H, 2))
print(round(L, 2))
print(round(eta, 1))

traps: Splitting an unsorted Shannon-Fano list. The rule assumes decreasing order; a valid but poor code can result.
Reporting one symbol's codeword length as the average length. L̄ is the probability-weighted sum Σ pᵢ lᵢ, not a single lᵢ.
Mixing natural logs with base-2 lengths. Use base 2 for both; answers are in bits per symbol.
Writing redundancy as H(X)/L̄. Efficiency is H(X)/L̄; redundancy is 1 − H(X)/L̄.

quiz.a: A prefix code is a set of binary codewords in which no codeword is a prefix of another codeword.

quiz.q: Why does a prefix code allow instant decoding without commas or lookahead?
quiz.a: The receiver scans bits from the start. As soon as the bits match a complete codeword, no longer codeword can begin with that same bit string, so the symbol is known immediately. No extra separator bit is needed.

quiz.q: A source has probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. Build a Huffman code and find L̄ and η.
quiz.a: Merge 0.25 and 0.25 into 0.5, then merge the two 0.5 nodes. Codes: 0, 10, 11. Lengths: 1, 2, 2. L̄ = 0.5(1) + 0.25(2) + 0.25(2) = 1.5 bits/symbol. H(X) = 1.5 bits/symbol, so η = 100%.

quiz.q: A sorted probability list is 0.35, 0.25, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1. A student splits it as {0.35, 0.25} and {0.2, 0.1, 0.1}. Comment on the split.
quiz.a: The group sums are 0.60 and 0.40, a difference of 0.20. That is the closest split here: {0.35} against the rest gives 0.35 and 0.65, and {0.35, 0.25, 0.2} against the rest gives 0.80 and 0.20. The student's split is acceptable for Shannon-Fano.

quiz.q: State the source coding theorem for a prefix code.
quiz.a: For a source of entropy H(X) bits per symbol and a prefix code of average length L̄ bits per symbol, H(X) ≤ L̄. For one symbol at a time, a prefix code exists with L̄ < H(X) + 1; for a block of n symbols, the gap is less than 1/n.

quiz.q: Why can Huffman coding beat Shannon-Fano on some sources?
quiz.a: Huffman merges the two smallest probabilities at every step and is optimal among binary prefix codes with integer lengths. Shannon-Fano only makes a local split into nearly equal probability groups; a poor split can give a valid but longer average length.

quiz.q: Is the code {0, 01, 11} a prefix code? What goes wrong in decoding?
quiz.a: No. Codeword 0 is a prefix of codeword 01. After receiving 0, the receiver cannot tell whether the symbol for 0 has arrived or whether the next bit will complete 01. The code needs lookahead and is not instantaneously decodable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Canonical Huffman codes send the code table compactly. DEFLATE, used in ZIP and gzip, combines LZ77 with Huffman coding. JPEG and MP3 use Huffman tables. Arithmetic coding and asymmetric numeral systems beat Huffman at very low bit rates because they avoid the integer-length gap.
